newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: INTERVIEW-Argentine opposition vows parity to stay.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Argentine opposition vows parity to stay.

text.p: The Argentine opposition alliance's main economic spokesman on Friday said the current system pegging the peso to the dollar would stay in place for the foreseeable future, no matter who was in power.

Jose Luis Machinea said in an interview with Reuters Financial Television that he could not imagine conditions in the next few years that would allow the "Convertibility" currency board system of peso-dollar parity to be modified.

"I think that if the alliance has to govern Argentina from 1999 on, or if the candidate of the government has to govern Argentina at that time, neither one nor the other would alter Convertibility," he said.

Under the Convertibility system, Argentina's peso has been pegged at par with the dollar since 1991, when a law was passed forbidding the central bank from printing money unless it was fully backed by foreign currency or gold reserves.

Machinea also said that the alliance formed by the centrist Radical Party and the center-left Frepaso at the beginning of August would perserve free-market reforms put in place by President Carlos Menem's Peronist government.
But he pledged more attention to social services and a drive to reduce corruption and reform the country's court system if the alliance won presidential elections due in 1999.

"We want to maintain the deficit reduction. We want to maintain Convertibility. But at the same time there are a lot of (workers) with a lot of problems," he said. "Therefore, we think we have to put more effort on...social expenditure."

Machinea was critical of the way the government has pursued the task of opening an economy closed to the world for decades, and he said it was responsible for the country's high unemployment rate, which currently stands at 16.1 percent.

"The problem has not been Convertibility, but perhaps the way in which this economy was opened to foreign imports," he said. "This is not a problem of opening up the economy. The problem is how you open the economy, and this economy was opened from one day to the other."
The alliance would seek to create jobs and generate more economic growth by providing more incentives to exporters.

"We do need to discuss with the workers in order to have a kind of consensus in order to go to the Congress and to have a reform by law," he said. "Because if we don't have this...we have this law by decree that will be changed any time in the near future."
Opposition to a package of proposed labor reforms was one of the triggers for a general strike staged by some unions on Thursday.
Asked to define the alliance's political leanings, Machinea referred to Britain's Labour Party Prime Minister Tony Blair.
"Tony Blair what is? Right or left?" he said.
